hints.title: Express the equal areas through central angles
hints.body: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> be the circle radius and let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> be a triangle angle at the centre. Express the triangle area using its two radius sides and their included angle.
hints.recap: All radius sides have the same length, and the central angles add to a full turn.
hints.pitfall: Equal triangle areas need not immediately imply equal included angles.
hints.pause: Translate the equal-area condition into a condition on the central angles.

recall.reminder: Use one half of the product of two sides and the sine of their included angle.

hints.title: Retain the second sine branch
hints.body: The centre is inside the polygon, so each consecutive central angle is between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math>. Within this interval, angles with a given sine can be equal or supplementary.
hints.recap: The identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> permits two angle sizes.
hints.pitfall: A regular polygon requires equal central angle gaps, so check whether the supplementary alternative is possible.
hints.pause: Describe all central angles using the two possible sizes and impose their total.

recall.reminder: Retain every angle branch allowed by the domain.

hints.title: Separate the small and general cases
hints.body: Investigate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> separately. Count how many central angles use each allowed size; seek an unequal-angle configuration whenever the total-angle equation permits one.
hints.recap: A sufficiency claim needs a proof for every allowed configuration, while a counterexample needs only one valid nonregular polygon.
hints.pitfall: A proposed counterexample must retain the centre inside and all the radial triangle areas equal.
hints.pause: For each n case, either prove that all angle gaps must coincide or construct and check a nonregular example.

recall.reminder: Test every geometric condition when constructing a counterexample.

solution:
Let the common radius be R. A radial triangle with central angle θ has area 12R2sinθ. Since the centre is inside, each angle lies in (0,π), and the angles sum to 2π. Equal areas therefore allow angles α or π−α, where 0<α≤π/2.

For three angles, a mixture with one larger angle sums to π+α<2π, and one with two larger angles sums to 2π−α<2π. Three acute or right angles also cannot total 2π. Thus all three must be equal to 2π/3, and the triangle is equilateral.

For four vertices, any nonsquare rectangle is a counterexample: it is cyclic, its centre is inside, and the four central triangles have equal area.

For any n≥5, choose α=π/(n−2). Use n−1 central angles equal to α and one equal to π−α. They sum to (n−2)α+π=2π, lie strictly between 0 and π, and have equal sine. The resulting cyclic polygon contains the centre and has unequal angle gaps, so is not regular.

Only n=3 is sufficient. Answer: B.
knowledgePattern: Use supplementary central-angle alternatives and construct nonregular cases
